h1: Traffic Ticket Dismissal in El Paso, Texas
intro: A dismissal is the best result a traffic ticket can have: no conviction, no points, nothing reported to DPS or your insurer. Attorney Robert Navar looks for every legal ground for dismissal in every El Paso County ticket we handle, for a flat fee from $59.
summary: A dismissal ends the case with no conviction and no record, while deferred disposition is a dismissal that comes only after you complete a 90–180 day violation-free period and pay a court fee.

The grounds we use most in El Paso: defective citations, the officer not appearing, insufficient evidence, radar or lidar calibration gaps, the wrong statute cited, and compliance dismissals for insurance, registration and license tickets.
An outright dismissal means nothing is reported to DPS, no points are assessed, and your insurance company has nothing to rate.

No lawyer can promise a dismissal. We work for one first, and if it is not available we secure the next best result — a deferral or a non-moving reduction — so the ticket still never becomes a conviction.

sections.heading: What a Traffic Ticket Dismissal Actually Means
paragraphs: When a Class C traffic case is dismissed, the prosecutor withdraws the charge or the judge orders it dropped, and the case closes with no finding of guilt. The court sends nothing to the Texas Department of Public Safety, so no conviction appears on your driving record, no points are added and your insurer never learns about the stop. It is the first result we ask for on every docket, whether the case is in El Paso Municipal Court, a county JP precinct or one of the smaller city courts.

People often confuse a dismissal with deferred disposition, and the two are different. Deferred disposition under Code of Criminal Procedure art. 45.051 is a conditional outcome: you pay a special expense fee, stay violation-free for 90 to 180 days, and only then is the case dismissed. A true dismissal needs no fee, no waiting period and no conditions. Our deferred adjudication and defensive driving page explains when deferral is the right fallback.

sections.heading: Defective Citations and the Wrong Statute
paragraphs: A traffic citation is a charging document, and it has to say what offense you are accused of, where, when and under what law. Errors are common: a Transportation Code section that does not match the described conduct, a missing or impossible speed, a location that is outside the officer's jurisdiction, a wrong date, or a description so vague the prosecutor cannot prove the elements. When the citation charges the wrong statute — a 545.351 speeding charge for conduct that was really something else, for example — the prosecutor has to amend or dismiss, and amendment is not always possible once the case is on a docket.

We read every citation before the first setting. In El Paso Municipal Court, where the city prosecutor handles hundreds of cases per docket, a clear defect pointed out by counsel is often enough for a dismissal on the spot; the office would rather dismiss a flawed ticket than set it for trial.

sections.heading: Officer No-Shows, Lack of Evidence and Radar Calibration
paragraphs: If a case is not resolved at pretrial, it is set for trial, and at trial the State must bring the officer to testify. Officers retire, transfer, get reassigned or have a conflict; DPS troopers in particular move around the state. When the officer does not appear for a trial setting, we ask the court to dismiss, and most El Paso County judges will.

Even with the officer present, the State needs evidence of each element. For a speeding ticket that usually means a radar or lidar reading, and the device has to have been calibrated and tested on schedule, with the officer trained to use it. An officer who cannot produce the calibration log for the date of your stop has a problem proving the speed. For red light and stop sign tickets the question is often whether the officer had a clear view of the line. We raise these gaps with the prosecutor at pretrial, where they are leverage for a dismissal even without a trial.

sections.heading: Compliance Dismissals: Insurance, Registration and License Tickets
paragraphs: A large share of El Paso tickets are not about driving at all but about paperwork: failure to maintain financial responsibility under Transportation Code 601.191, expired registration or inspection, and no driver's license under 521.021. Texas law and local practice favor dismissing these once the driver fixes the problem.

Courts in El Paso County routinely dismiss a no-insurance ticket on proof of a policy in effect on the stop date, dismiss a registration or inspection ticket when the renewal is completed within the time the court allows, and dismiss a no-license ticket when the driver obtains a license. We tell new clients exactly what to fix and when, then present the proof to the prosecutor so the case closes as a dismissal rather than a deferral.

sections.heading: What a Dismissal Means for DPS, Insurance and Your Record
paragraphs: After a dismissal the court closes the case and reports no conviction. Your DPS driving record shows nothing from the stop, no points accrue toward the suspension thresholds, and insurers — who rate from the driving record and claims history — have nothing to see. The arrest or citation itself may still exist in the court's own records, and for drivers who want that gone too, a Class C dismissal may qualify for an expunction under Code of Criminal Procedure Chapter 55A.

Realistic expectations matter. Not every ticket has a defect, not every officer misses court, and we will never tell you a dismissal is guaranteed. What we can say is that we look for every ground on every case, and that when a dismissal is not available the fallback — deferred disposition or a non-moving reduction — still keeps a conviction off your record in most cases. For a longer walkthrough, read our blog post on finding a traffic ticket dismissal.

sections.heading: How to Give Your Ticket the Best Chance of Dismissal
paragraphs: Do not pay the ticket and do not request defensive driving on your own — both are pleas that end the case as a conviction or a deferral before anyone has looked for a dismissal. Keep the citation, note the appearance date, and fix any compliance problem right away. Then hire us online or call 915-503-1600; our flat fee is $59 in El Paso Municipal Court and $69 in the JP and area city courts, and the consultation is free.

This page is general information, not legal advice about your case. Whether a dismissal is realistic depends on the citation, the court and the facts, and we are glad to look at yours before you decide anything.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a dismissal and deferred disposition?
faqs.a: A dismissal ends the case immediately with no conviction. Deferred disposition under art. 45.051 requires a court fee and a 90–180 day violation-free period, after which the case is dismissed. Both avoid a conviction, but a true dismissal costs less and carries no conditions.

faqs.q: What are the most common reasons an El Paso ticket gets dismissed?
faqs.a: Defects in the citation, the officer not appearing for trial, missing evidence such as radar calibration records, the wrong statute cited, and compliance dismissals for insurance, registration and license tickets after the driver fixes the problem.

faqs.q: Does a dismissed ticket go on my driving record?
faqs.a: No. The court reports no conviction to DPS, so nothing appears on your driving record, no points are assessed and your insurer has nothing to rate. The court's own file may still show the citation, which an expunction can address.

faqs.q: Can you guarantee my ticket will be dismissed?
faqs.a: No lawyer can. We pursue a dismissal first on every case, and dismissals are a routine result in El Paso County, but when one is not available we work for deferred disposition or a non-moving reduction so the ticket still does not become a conviction.

faqs.q: I had insurance but didn't have the card with me. Can the ticket be dismissed?
faqs.a: Usually, yes. Proof that a valid policy was in force on the stop date generally results in a dismissal of a failure-to-maintain-financial-responsibility ticket. Send us the declarations page and we present it to the prosecutor.

faqs.q: How long does a dismissal take?
faqs.a: Compliance dismissals can happen at the first docket setting, often within a few weeks. Dismissals that depend on an officer no-show take longer, sometimes a few months, because the case must first be set for trial.
